passages.original: L Qua in re substantiæ quoque est reddita definitio: nam si nomen naturæ substantiam monstrat, cum naturam descripsimus, substantiae quoque est assignata descriptio. Quod si naturae nomen, relictis in. corporeis substantiis, ad corporales usque, ut cor. poreaetantum _substantisenaturamhaberevideantur. sicut Aristoteles caeterique ejusmodi et multimodae philosophiae sectatores putant,definiemus eam ut hi etiam qui naturam non nisi in corporibus esse posuerunt. Est autem ejus definitio hoc modo : Natura est motus principium, secundum se, non per accidens.
passages.english: In this the definition of substance has also been given: for if the name "nature" designates substance, then when we described nature, a description of substance was also assigned. But if the name "nature" is carried, leaving incorporeal substances aside, down to corporeal ones, so that only corporeal substances seem to have a nature, as Aristotle and the other followers of that and of many kinds of philosophy think, we shall define it as those also [define it] who have held that nature exists only in bodies. Its definition is as follows: Nature is the principle of motion in itself, not by accident.
passages.notes: The initial "L" appears to be a stray mark or section numeral and is omitted. Scanning errors corrected: "in. corporeis" for incorporeis, "cor. poreaetantum _substantisenaturamhaberevideantur" for corporeae tantum substantiae naturam habere videantur. "et multimodae philosophiae sectatores" is odd; perhaps "hujusmodi et multimodae" is corrupt; translated literally.

passages.original: Universales sunt quae de singulis praedicantur, ut homo, animal, lapis,lignum caeteraque hujusmodi quae vel genera vel species sunt: nam ethomo desingulishominibus, et animal de singulis animalibus, lapisque ac lignum de sinulis lapidibus ac lignis dicuntur. Particularia vero sunt quae de aliis minime praedicantur, ut Cicero, Plato, lapis hic unde hæc Achillis statua facta est ; lignum hoc unde haec mensa composita est. Sed in his omnibus nusquam in universalibus persona dici potest, sed in singularibus tantum atque in individuis : animalis enim vel generalis hominis nulla persona est, sed vel Ciceronis vel Platonis vel singulorum individuorum personæ singulae nuncupantur.
passages.english: Universal [substances] are those which are predicated of individual things, such as man, animal, stone, wood, and the other things of this kind which are either genera or species; for "man" is said of individual men, "animal" of individual animals, and "stone" and "wood" of individual stones and pieces of wood. Particular [substances], on the other hand, are those which are not predicated of other things at all, such as Cicero, Plato, this stone from which this statue of Achilles was made, this wood from which this table was put together. But in all these, "person" can nowhere be said of universals, but only of singulars and individuals: for there is no person of animal or of man in general, but it is only of Cicero or of Plato or of each individual that single persons are spoken of.

passages.english: For they are already informed by their proper and specific differences and accidents, and they supply [to accidents the means] by which these can exist, namely while they are subjects. Therefore *einai* and *ousiōsthai* are understood as "to be" and "to subsist," while *hyphistasthai* is understood as "to stand under." For Greece is not poor in words, as Marcus Tullius jokingly suggests; rather, it renders essence, subsistence, substance and person with as many names, calling essence *ousia*, subsistence *ousiōsis*, substance *hypostasis*, and person *prosōpon*. And the Greeks called individual substances *hypostaseis* for this reason: because they stand under the rest, and are placed under and subject to certain things, accidents as it were;
passages.notes: The Greek is badly garbled by the scan: "οὐσιωαι" read as οὐσιῶσθαι (to subsist); "ouatav" as οὐσίαν; "oua£ωοιν" as οὐσίωσιν; "ὐποστάσις" as ὑποστάσεις. The clause "uteese possint ministrant" is read as "ut esse possint, ministrant" (they supply [accidents with that by which] they can be); the construction is compressed and the bracketed supplement is interpretive. The allusion to Cicero (Marcus Tullius) concerns his claim that Latin is richer in vocabulary than Greek.
